Class "dbartsSampler" of Discrete Bayesian Additive Regression Trees Sampler

dbartsSampler-class.Rd

A reference class object that contains a Bayesian Additive Regression Trees sampler in such a way that it can be modified, stopped, and started all while maintaining its own state.

Note

dbartsSampler is a reference class: its methods are not called as free functions but as $-dispatched calls on a sampler instance, e.g. sampler$run(100, 100) or sampler$setResponse(newY). The S4-method notation in ‘Usage’ below is an artifact of how reference-class methods are documented and does not reflect the calling syntax; see ‘Examples’.

Arguments

numBurnIn

A non-negative integer determining how many iterations the sampler should skip before storing results. If NULL (the default), it is filled in from the sampler's control object; an explicit NA reads as NULL for one release, with a once-per-session warning.

numSamples

A positive integer determining how many posterior samples should be returned. If NULL (the default), it is also filled in from the control object; an explicit NA reads as NULL for one release, with a once-per-session warning.

callback

NULL (the default) or a list with two elements, fn and context, each an R external pointer (externalptr): fn the address of a compiled dbarts_draw_callback (inst/include/dbarts/dbarts.h) and context an opaque pointer handed back to it unchanged, or NULL. It fires once per SAVED draw of this call, per chain, on the thread that owns that chain, over const pointers into this run's own result buffers or, for a channel this run does not keep, into a per-chain one-draw scratch buffer the chain's next draw overwrites: the per-observation channels under control@keepFits == FALSE, and always the draw's log-likelihood, which this run never returns and computes only for the callback. A nonzero return aborts the run. A draw's sigma is NaN on a sampler with a variance forest, which reports the variance channels instead. Only that both list elements are external pointers is checked - the address is dereferenced exactly as handed, so a malformed pair or a stale pointer crashes the session with no condition to catch. Registering one is a compiled task (Rcpp or plain C), not an R closure: see vignette("dbarts-as-a-component"). Three warnings. A callback that crashes takes the whole session down with it. An interrupt (Ctrl-C) cannot land while a call is running, so a callback that blocks or loops hangs the session. And under control@keepFits == FALSE the per-observation channels this call returns are NULL - present in the returned list, holding nothing - so whatever the callback itself accumulated is the only record of the run's per-observation fits. On a family = "hazard"/"hazard.probit"/"hazard.logistic" sampler the draw struct's numObservations counts the person-period-EXPANDED rows, one per subject per at-risk period, not the original subjects; the row-to-(subject, period) mapping is built in R and is not carried across to the callback. A hook set through the flat C entry dbarts_sampler_setDrawCallback does NOT fire on this route: bartcore_run (which this method calls) builds its own per-run hook from THIS argument, so the two channels are independent - a C caller mixing both must register the same callback on each to see it fire on both.

updateState

A logical determining if the local cache of the sampler's state should be updated after the call completes. One convention applies to every method that takes this argument - run, sampleTreesFromPrior, sampleLeafParametersFromPrior, sampleVarianceForestFromPrior, growFromRoot, and every mutator (setData, setResponse, setOffset, setWeights, setCategoryOffset, setActiveRows, setForestWeights, setForestBasis, setSigma, setLeafPrior, setPredictor, and setCutPoints): NULL (the default) resolves to the sampler's control object's updateState, and an explicit TRUE or FALSE, or a single number read as as.logical reads it (0 is FALSE), overrides it. Anything else is an error, raised before the sampler changes; an explicit NA, the default of 0.9-x, reads as NULL for one release, with a once-per-session warning. The mutators are typically called once per sweep inside a larger Gibbs/MH loop (as dbartsSampler is designed for); a control with updateState = FALSE keeps such a loop free of the store's cost on every call, while the default TRUE keeps state current after each one. Under control@updateState = TRUE the first read of a state no store has yet filled stores the sampler's current state, so a mutate-then-first-read sequence needs no explicit store; under FALSE that first read is NULL, and $storeState() makes the store. Pass TRUE explicitly to force a store under a control@updateState = FALSE sampler, or FALSE to skip one under control@updateState = TRUE.

shallow

A logical determining if the copy should retain the underlying data of the sampler (TRUE) or have its own copies (FALSE). Either way, the copy keeps the original's model and its data object, on whose record of the cut points, their weights and the response range it is built (see dbartsData). A copy of a sampler whose engine exists in this R session takes that engine's current chain, as stored, converting nothing, whatever the original's state field holds, and the copy's state field is that chain; the original's own field and draws are untouched. A copy of one whose engine is gone, as after a load, installs its stored state as a reload does, and without one is refused, as a reload is (see ‘Saving’). Either way it continues the same generator streams as the original - not an independent chain - typically matching an uninterrupted run to the last few digits, not bitwise; see the Reproducibility section of bart. When n.samples was changed after the chain was stored, the copy's saved-tree store takes the chain's capacity, as a reload does, and keeps the saved trees it holds rather than truncating or resetting them.

newControl

An object inheriting from dbartsControl. When passed to setControl, it cannot change n.chains or seed from the values the sampler was created with, a n.trees, useQuantiles or n.cuts its caller wrote cannot differ from the sampler's, and it cannot set keepTrees = TRUE without also giving n.samples; each is an error. A control taken from another fit that holds another of those three is taken with a warning, and a fresh control silently, the sampler keeping its own. Under treeShift = "auto" the step follows the mixture, which setControl may freeze, on every forest that states no mixture of its own.

newModel

An object inheriting from dbartsModel. When passed to setModel, it changes the numbers inside the sampler's model and is refused, by name and before anything is stored, where it differs in structure: the response family (a Student-t error against a Gaussian one included), the kind of leaf and its covariate columns, a Gaussian-process leaf's max.leaf.size, the interaction limits and blocks, DART against the ordinary tree prior, the columns a forest may split on (its forest vars), the tree count of a forest or the variance forest, and the monotone directions; make a new sampler instead. A count the model does not state, as in dbartsSpec(data, power = 3)$model, leaves the sampler's. It takes power and base, the split probabilities, the leaf scale as k or sd, the residual prior, the Student-t degrees of freedom, a negative-binomial shape, a Gaussian-process lengthscale and DART's own settings. A degrees of freedom, shape or DART alpha handed from held to drawn starts at the value in force, not where a new sampler would start it; a new lengthscale is refused on a sampler holding kept draws, which replay only under the kernel they were drawn with. A model that states no family, degrees of freedom or lengthscale keeps the sampler's. A split probability of zero on a column some chain's trees split on is refused, naming the column. A residual prior other than the sampler's own is refused on a family with no residual scale (probit, logistic, ordinal, negative binomial, hazard), a chisq() residual prior of df 2 or below on a sampler whose variance forest has two or more trees, each tree's prior being calibrated to the prior mean of \(\sigma^2\), which is infinite there, and so is a model whose leaf prior's k or sd does not resolve to the leaf hyperprior and prior scale it carries: setLeafPrior restates a leaf prior. The sampler's own model, as after setResponse or setOffset, is always accepted. On a sampler of several forests or a multinomial one it takes the fitting function's level, as setTreePrior and setLeafPrior write it: a changed power or base reaches the forests with no basis that state none of their own, and, where one forest has no basis, or on a multinomial sampler's category forests, those forests whatever they state; the leaf prior goes where setLeafPrior sends it; and the residual prior is installed as on one forest. A number a forest's record in the model states, a mean forest's own sd, power or base or the variance forest's power or base, is installed where it differs from the sampler's, through the code setForest or setVarianceForest runs on that forest, so the sampler runs as after that call; the later write wins between this and those methods. A number the record does not state is left as it is: dbartsSpec(data, power = 2.5, variance = varianceForest())$model moves the mean forest's depth and leaves the variance forest's, which only copied the mean depth at creation, and a forest that states its own on the sampler keeps it. A forest's coefficient's prior that differs is refused, naming setForest; so is a leaf scale other than the sampler's, split probabilities other than equal ones, and a forest's sd whose sharers' parts of the prior total then differ from the model's. A new fixed negative-binomial shape keeps the latents in force. This draws nothing; the next sweep draws the augmentation variables against the change.

newData

An object inheriting from dbartsData. A sampler created with one forest and none refuses data that carry bases, having no forest to multiply them; make a new sampler from such data with dbarts. Columns are matched by name: the new data carry the sampler's names, in any order, and names that are not the sampler's are refused, as predict refuses them, leaving the sampler as it was. A matrix with no column names is read by position, with no message, as is any data handed to a sampler that has none, whose record then takes the data's names, which predict needs; a sampler whose names repeat takes the same names in the same places only. A factor column is read by label against the levels the sampler was created with, which it keeps: fewer levels, the levels in another order and declared levels no row has are taken, each row at its own label; a row, training or test, at a label the sampler never had is refused by name, as predict refuses one, and so is a factor column given as numbers with no level table. A factor whose labels were changed on purpose is relabeled to the sampler's labels first, with levels<-, or given to a new sampler. A column that could hold missing values before the call still can, and one the new data first give a missing value becomes able to, as ‘Missing values in predictors’ in ‘Details’ describes. The cut points, the response range and a linear or gp leaf's covariate standardization follow updateCutPoints, updateScale and updateStandardization; with each left at NULL, a value newData records (its cutPoints, response.range and standardization slots, see dbartsData) is used and one it does not record is derived from it. A cut count or quantile rule newData states wins over the sampler's (see n.cuts and useQuantiles on dbartsData), and the sampler derives by what it takes from then on, in this call and in any later refresh; an object carrying cutPoints brings the count and rule that made them, an unstated rule reading as even; an object stating neither keeps the sampler's, a count stated to dbartsData() is read over the predictors the sampler holds, a hazard sampler's period column among them, which takes a count only by its own name and is otherwise 100, and updateCutPoints = "none" keeps the sampler's whatever the object states. The sampler writes its values into its own data object, so sampler$setData(sampler$data), the object handed back whole, keeps the cut points, the range and the standardization the sampler held, where 0.9-x derived them again; to change a column and keep them, sampler$setPredictor(newValues, 1, forceUpdate = TRUE) takes the values and keeps the cut points and the record; and a data object made by dbartsData records none and derives every one, as before. Draws the sampler has saved (keepTrees) stay the functions they were, so predict returns the same values for them before and after the call. To that end a linear leaf's coefficients, saved and current, are rewritten into the center and scale the call derives or takes for its leaf covariates, and every saved draw into the response scale it derives or takes; a value kept, or taken equal to the one in force, rewrites nothing. A row whose leaf covariate is missing is read at that covariate's center, so what a linear leaf predicts for it follows the center to the new data's. A standardization the call derives is read over the new data's rows in the likelihood, those of positive weight; where fewer than two rows are in (subjects, for a hazard fit, whose data hold each subject's rows together, at periods 1, 2, 3 and on in order, as dbarts expands them, data laid out otherwise being refused), or the call reads the response's scale from every row because those rows hold fewer than two distinct values of it, the leaf covariates are read from every row, under one warning; where the rows read hold one value of a leaf covariate, or observe none, the call is refused before anything changes, unless a gp leaf states its lengthscale, and updateStandardization = FALSE takes the data under the sampler's own. Under such a family the sampler's own data object carries no weights, so setData(sampler$data) drops the mask in force: hand the 0/1 weights back on the data object, or call setActiveRows after. A leaf covariate that holds a single value is centered at it and divided by 1, so a leaf reads zero for it on every row and its slope adds nothing to the fit. Where a covariate is such a column on one side of the call only, the current coefficients are still rewritten by the formula, with 1 for that side's scale, so each leaf keeps its function of the covariate: onto such a column it takes the value its function has at the new constant, and off one the slope no row informed is carried onto the new data's spread, so the fit may move until the sampler has run on them. Where it is such a column on both sides the current coefficients are left as they are. A column that setPredictor has since given other values is read as what it then holds: one moved to another single value no longer sits at its center and is rewritten as any other column is, by the formula, which keeps the function of the covariate. The data fixed that function at one point only, so new data that spread the covariate widely can carry the current fit far from where it was until the sampler has run on them. Saved draws are rewritten by the formula in every case, with 1 for the scale. The saved draws of a Gaussian-process (gp) leaf cannot be rewritten: a sampler with such leaves that holds saved draws refuses a call that would derive the standardization or the range, as one given a data object that records neither does, or that would take a recorded one other than its own; it takes one that keeps both, as setData(sampler$data) or updateStandardization = FALSE, updateScale = FALSE do, whatever cut points it is given, a saved draw holding its thresholds by value. Pass those two, or make a new sampler. A family with no response range (probit, ordinal, logistic) has none to change. One that holds no saved draw takes any call as any other sampler does. The ordinal cutpoints, the Student-t degrees of freedom and the negative-binomial shape the sampler has drawn are kept, as are its trees, and the latents start as creation starts them, the number of rows possibly differing (an ordinal or negative-binomial sampler from the kept cutpoints or shape); the next sweep draws them from the kept values. This draws nothing; the next sweep draws the augmentation variables against the change.

y

A numeric response vector, or on a count sampler the matrix below, of length equal to that with which the sampler was created, and lying in the response family's support: 0/1 for probit and logistic, an integer category index in \([1, K]\) for ordinal, and a finite non-negative integer count no larger than \(10^6\) for nbinom (the shape grid's count histogram is sized from the largest count, so a larger one allocates without bound). Values off the support are refused, as they are at creation; gaussian and aft (log survival times) constrain nothing. A missing value is refused in every family: to leave a row out of the likelihood mid-chain, mark it inactive with setActiveRows and give it any value in the support, which enters no draw while the row stays inactive unless the call re-anchors the scale (updateScale = TRUE), which reads the rows in the likelihood. On a multinomial (softmax) sampler y is its response as its formula writes it: an \(n \times K\) matrix of non-negative integer counts, column \(k\) holding category \(k\)'s successes, with trials \(n_i = \sum_k\) y[i, ] at least 0 and no larger than \(10^6\): a row with no trial enters no likelihood and still receives fitted probabilities, and the first such row in a session warns. Both \(n\) and \(K\) are fixed at creation - every combiner buffer is sized by \(n\), and \(K\) is the forest count - so only the values may change; a matrix of the wrong shape is refused naming the count in force. The trees carry over, fitted to the previous counts exactly as setResponse leaves any sampler's, and the next run forms every category's working response against the new matrix. The matrix is written to both the engine and data@counts (its row sums to data@y), so getPointer's transparent re-creation after save and load carries the current response rather than the one the sampler was created with. Cost, not a defect: the sweep draws \(n_i\) Polya-Gamma variates per observation per category, so replacing single-trial labels with grouped counts multiplies sweep cost by mean(n_i). A missing count is refused, as a missing response is; to leave a row out of the likelihood mid-chain, mark it inactive with setActiveRows, as in every family, or write zeros into it, which is the same as far as the likelihood goes. A vector is refused there, since with each row's trials held it cannot say how they split among the categories. On a binomial sampler, a logistic one whose data carry the response as counts of successes and failures, y is the \(n \times 2\) matrix of successes and failures, or a vector of successes with each row's trials held, a count above its row's trials refused; setData takes new data whose counts give both, the number of rows free. A count sampler has no response scale to re-anchor and ignores updateScale. This draws nothing; the next sweep draws the augmentation variables against the change.

status

For setResponse on an aft (survival) sampler, a replacement per-observation censoring status: a numeric vector of length equal to that with which the sampler was created, 1 an uncensored event and 0 a right-censored observation whose response value is its truncation lower bound. NULL (the default) leaves the censoring structure in force and is the call every other family makes; a non-null status on any other family is refused by name. The response and the status change in ONE call, and the status is installed first, so a row newly censored is bounded at its own NEW observed log time and held there until the next sweep draws it above that bound against the fit then in force, as setResponse leaves every censored row at its new bound, while a row that becomes an event is restored to that time - data, rather than a draw. A status-only change is setResponse(sampler$data@y, status = s). The number of observations is fixed, the status being stated over it; setData, whose replacement may change it, refuses an aft sampler and names this channel instead. The vector is validated - real, of length \(n\), every element exactly 0 or 1, NA refused - before anything installs, so a refused call leaves the sampler, data@y and the recorded status exactly as they were; it is written to the sampler's data object only after the engine accepts it, so getPointer's re-creation after save and load carries the current censoring rather than the one the sampler was created with. Under an installed mask (active) the response install is mask-blind but the sweep's draw is not, so an INACTIVE censored row's latent stays at its bound until the mask clears; that is what setResponse leaves such a row at with or without a status.

x

For setPredictor with no column, the whole of the predictors: a data frame, whose columns are matched to the sampler's by name, in any order, a name that is not the sampler's being refused (a sampler with no names reads them by position), and whose factor columns are coded by label as a column update's are, or a numeric matrix, taken only where every predictor column is numeric - on a sampler with a factor column a matrix is refused by name, since its codes could not say which values are labels. A matrix that carries column names is matched by name as a frame is, and one with none is read by position, with no message. Otherwise, a numeric predictor vector of length equal to that with which the sampler was created. Can be of a distinct number of rows for setTestPredictor. A column update (column given) on a column coded from a factor takes that column's labels instead, for setPredictor and setTestPredictor alike: a factor, character vector or sparseFactor, matched by label against the training levels, as a whole data-frame update is coded; several columns take a data frame. A label the column does not declare is refused by name, as is a number, which could only be read as an internal code. A missing label is a missing value: setPredictor takes it whether or not the column has held one, and setTestPredictor refuses a missing value, a label or a number, in a column that has never held one in training, as the whole test set is refused. What a column's first missing value does is under ‘Missing values in predictors’ in ‘Details’. On a hazard fit, setPredictor takes the period column, whole, as a column or row by row ("partial"), only unchanged, refusing any other values before anything moves: the column is the expansion of each subject's time at risk, set with the response, and setData replaces it. setPredictor draws nothing: the next sweep draws the augmentation variables against the accepted predictors.

x.test

A new matrix, data frame, or sparse-bearing test set (the column types accepted by dbartsData), of the number of columns equal to that in the current model; a numeric matrix is taken only where every predictor column is numeric, and is refused by name on a sampler with a factor column, whose test rows come as a data frame (the same holds for predict on a fit). A data-frame/sparse x.test is coded against the training levels; setTestPredictor and setTestPredictorAndOffset then install it as a resident, whole-object replacement of the test set (see column), while predict and predictForests route its rows through the trees off that same storage, retaining nothing.

offset

A numeric vector of length equal to that with which the sampler was created, or NULL. If offset.test was set from offset, will attempt to update that as well.

For setCategoryOffset, a multinomial sampler's per-category shift instead: an \(n \times K\) numeric matrix, or NULL to clear one. The latent becomes \(f_{ik} + o_{ik}\), so the shift enters the log-sum-exp margins, every category's working response and the reported probabilities, and never a leaf value. This is the response-side counterpart of setResponse's count matrix rather than of setOffset, whose flat shift is added AFTER the categories are blended - the wrong side of the nonlinearity - and is the softmax's own null direction besides, which is why setOffset itself is refused on such a sampler. Only the row-centered part is identified: adding a constant to a whole row leaves every reported probability unchanged, and the entrance leaves the matrix as given rather than re-centering it. It shifts the TRAINING latent only. Mirrored into data@offset.category, so a re-created sampler carries it. Column names, when present, are matched to the sampler's category names (the column names of its counts; "1", ..., "K" when it has none): a permutation is reordered by name and other names are refused, except that a sampler without count column names reorders a permutation of its indices and ignores other names. Unnamed columns stay positional. setOffset draws nothing: the next sweep draws the augmentation variables against the new offset, on a logistic sampler as on every other family.

updateScale

Logical indicating whether BART's internal scale should re-anchor to the new offset (setOffset), response (setResponse), weights (setWeights) or active rows (setActiveRows). On the last two it is the argument after updateState, so the positional setWeights(w, TRUE) of earlier releases still names updateState. With TRUE they install the weights or the mask first and then take the response's scale (a count sampler's center) again from the rows then in the likelihood, as creation on those rows would, whether or not the call moved a row in or out; the response and the offset are not changed, and neither is a test offset, a cut point, a covariate standardization or the residual prior. Nothing is taken again by a one-forest probit, ordinal, logistic or hazard sampler, which accepts the argument and ignores it, also with gp leaves holding saved draws, none of which it moves. A call refused for any reason installs nothing; a call that keeps the scale (below) installs the weights or the mask. A stored state does not undo a re-derivation, and with updateState resolving to TRUE the state is stored after it. Defaults to FALSE, locking the scale set at creation; should only be TRUE during burn-in, as re-anchoring mid-run makes the fits across iterations no longer comparable. Draws already saved (keepTrees) are rewritten into the new scale, a heteroscedastic sampler's variance draws included, so predict returns the values it returned before the call; the current fit follows the new scale. TRUE is refused by a sampler with Gaussian-process (gp) leaves that holds saved draws, whatever the new response, offset, weights or mask, where its family has a scale to re-derive (gaussian, student, aft and nbinom): make a new sampler, or leave updateScale at FALSE. A probit, logistic or ordinal sampler has none, so it takes TRUE as it takes it in setData, and its saved draws predict what they did. A draw is saved by every sweep run as a sample while trees are kept, warm-up sweeps included, so such a sampler takes a re-anchor during burn-in only as long as its sweeps are run as burn-in, which saves nothing: run(1, 0) between re-anchors, not run(0, 1). For a survival (aft) sampler the scale is always that of the observed times, a censored row's censoring time among them, and never of a time the sampler has drawn for a censored row. TRUE is refused by a multi-forest (forests) sampler, whose calibration map is pinned at creation - whatever its response family, and whether or not there is a transform to re-anchor - and is never restated; the response and a basis scale may span different rows, which is why. setActiveRows(updateScale = TRUE) is refused by a multinomial sampler as its other response channels are. A heteroscedastic (variance) sampler takes it: the variance forest's leaf prior is re-derived from the residual prior on the new scale, exactly as creation on the new response would have stated it, and the drawn \(s^2(x)\) is carried into the same units, so the surface keeps its meaning in response units across the swap. setData carries that restatement too wherever the scale moves. On setData the argument defaults to NULL, which takes the response.range the new data object records and otherwise derives the scale; TRUE derives it from the new data, over its rows in the likelihood as creation would, and FALSE keeps the sampler's, the new response going in under it with no draw rewritten. A sampler made by hand from another's parts takes the record in the same way. Where rows are out and the rows in hold fewer than two distinct values of the response, a setData that derives the scale takes every row, under a warning of class dbartsScaleFallbackWarning; setResponse, setOffset, setWeights and setActiveRows with updateScale = TRUE instead keep the scale and the center in force, as with updateScale = FALSE, and warn with the same class once for a sampler (a copy or a reload is a new sampler, setData is not). On setResponse, supplying this argument positionally (setResponse(y, TRUE)) rather than by name warns once per session - it is the second argument, where a caller porting code written before this order had updateState there instead.

offset.test

A numeric vector of length equal to that of the test matrix, or NULL for no offset; a missing value is refused. Can be missing for setTestPredictorAndOffset. Refused, by name, for predictForests: an offset shifts the combination of the forests, exactly as the response transform's shift does, and neither is any one forest's own total.

For setCategoryTestOffset, a multinomial sampler's \(n_{\mathrm{test}} \times K\) per-category test shift, or NULL to clear one: the recorded test channel becomes \(\mathrm{softmax}(f_{\mathrm{test}} + o_{\mathrm{test}})\), formed where the training blend forms its own. The test fits enter no likelihood, so this moves the reported test probabilities and nothing else. Its rows are the CURRENT test rows, so replacing those rows while it is installed is refused rather than silently reinterpreted - clear it first - and out-of-sample predict does not read it at all, taking its own matrix for the rows it is given. Mirrored into data@offset.category.test. For predict on a multinomial sampler, likewise a per-category matrix, one row per PREDICTED row: a flat vector is refused there for the same reason, and a sampler holding either resident category offset refuses an unnamed call rather than reporting the offset-free surface, which an explicit all-zero matrix asks for on purpose. Column names, when present, are matched to the sampler's category names (the column names of its counts; "1", ..., "K" when it has none): a permutation is reordered by name and other names are refused, except that a sampler without count column names reorders a permutation of its indices and ignores other names. Unnamed columns stay positional.

n.threads

For predict and predictForests, a per-call worker count that does not persist, defaulting to the sampler's own (the n.threads of its control object, fixed at creation). The replay is partitioned by (chain, saved draw), each partition writing its own rows and nothing being reduced across workers, so the result is identical bit for bit at every value and only the time taken changes. A replay small enough that the partition could not pay for itself runs inline whatever is passed.

These are native threads, so _R_CHECK_LIMIT_CORES_ does not govern them: that variable is read only by parallel:::.check_ncores, which counts simultaneously spawned processes and never sees a thread.

run takes no thread count: a run uses the sampler's own, which setControl changes, and its draws are the same at every count.

sigma

A single positive residual standard deviation, on the original response scale; it is assigned to every chain. setSigma only applies to a sampler whose residual standard deviation is a free parameter: it is refused on a probit-, logistic-, multinomial-, ordinal-, or count-family sampler, which fix it at 1 by the model definition, and on a heteroscedastic (variance) sampler, whose variance forest owns the residual scale. A gaussian sampler with family = gaussian(sigma = fixed()) is not fixed in this sense and is still accepted: suppressing the internal draw so an outer sampler owns sigma is what that prior is for. There the write rewrites the model's fixed value, recorded on the model field, so a copy or a save and load keeps it; a write through the C API reaches the engine alone, and a sampler re-created after one holds the model's value until the next write. This draws nothing; the next sweep draws the augmentation variables against the change.

weights

A numeric vector of case weights, of length equal to that with which the sampler was created. What a weight MEANS is family-specific: for a gaussian-family sampler it is a precision, non-negative, or under weights.type = "frequency" (fixed at creation, see dbarts) a count of identical observations, real and non-negative, and a weight of zero takes an observation out of the likelihood and out of the residual degrees of freedom while keeping it in the design, its place in a leaf and its fitted values (see below); for a logistic-, nbinom- or multinomial-family sampler it is an observation COUNT and must be a non-negative whole number, no larger than \(10^6\) times the row's trials, \(y + r\) or row total, a count of 0 taking the row out of the likelihood: it consumes no random number, and the row draws as one masked by active does. A zero-weight row is IN THE DESIGN BUT NOT IN THE LIKELIHOOD, and takes no part in the response scale, the count center or a forest's default sd, which are taken over the rows of positive weight when the sampler is created (a row is in when its weight is positive and no mask switches it off) and held when the weights or the mask change, unless the call carries updateScale = TRUE, so the three ways to leave a row out - at creation, by setWeights or setActiveRows, and by subset - differ by when the row left. It counts as a member of its leaf, so the rule that rejects a tree move leaving a leaf empty counts it too: the trees a sampler may hold do not depend on the weights, and a leaf may hold zero-weight rows only, in which case no likelihood term reaches it and its value is a draw from the leaf prior. A fit with zero weights is therefore close to the fit on the remaining rows alone but is not that fit, since the trees can spend splits on regions of zero-weight rows. In one measured case, 300 rows with 50 trees and the cut points held equal and the scale that of the remaining rows: with a random half of the rows at weight zero the posterior mean fit at the remaining rows moved by at most 0.02 of a posterior standard deviation, and with a whole region at weight zero by at most 0.05; the residual standard deviation did not move, and the fit at the zero-weight rows was 1 to 2 percent more variable. dbartsData's subset drops rows outright, and with them their part in the cut points and the response scale. In exchange, an outer sampler that redraws 0/1 weights or active every sweep from its own conditional samples the joint model it assumes, which it would not if the admissible trees moved with the weights. A Student-t sampler holds a scale \(\lambda_i\) per row, which setWeights leaves as it is: the next sweep draws every scale from its conditional given the fit and the weights then in force, so an outer sampler that draws the weight given the scales and one that draws it with the scales integrated out are both exact. setWeights sets a weighted likelihood on gaussian-, logistic- and nbinom-family samplers. A logistic or nbinom swap is a model change with a defined meaning rather than a reweighting: the counts multiply the shape of the Polya-Gamma latents, which the next sweep draws against the new counts, so an outer sampler can vary exposure between runs. probit, ordinal and aft refuse a weighted likelihood by identification: a weighted probit has no tractable latent-variable form, ordinal inherits that, and aft fixes its censoring structure at creation. On a probit, ordinal or nbinom sampler a vector of 0s and 1s is accepted all the same: it names the rows in the data set rather than a precision, is held in the data object's weights slot, all ones as no weights, and composes with active below, a row being in when its weight is 1 and the mask keeps it; any other value keeps the refusal on probit and ordinal, and is a count on nbinom. setData carries the same rule on the whole-data conduit, the next sweep drawing the latents against the counts the replacement data carries; replacement data given without weights is single-trial, as at creation, so a logistic sampler built with counts and handed weightless data becomes an unweighted one. The weights themselves are not part of the saved state, and the state records nothing of them: the latents it carries are the values its trees were drawn from, which setState installs without drawing, and the next sweep draws them against the weights then in force. A weight change is undone by setWeights with the old weights and setState with the stored state, in either order, the sampler then continuing bit for bit as one that installed the stored state under the old weights would. This draws nothing; the next sweep draws the augmentation variables against the change. See dbarts for the family-specific weight rules that apply at creation time.

For setForestWeights, a distinct per-FOREST case weight on a Bayesian causal forest (built with forests = , see dbarts), refused off one: it composes with weights and active as \((w_i a_i) m_f^2 s_i\), where \(m_f\) is the named forest's own multiplier, rather than widening either channel, so s_i = 0 excludes row \(i\) from that forest's own leaf conditionals only - its occupancy, its place in the combination, and the residual degrees of freedom are unaffected, a leaf of that forest may hold such rows only (its value is then a draw from the leaf prior), and the reported location still carries the forest's full contribution even when every row is excluded. The third leg of a three-way degenerate-value contrast: weights at all-ones installs and, on gaussian and logistic, is measurably distinct from carrying none, active at all-ones installs nothing and clears any mask in force, and setForestWeights at all-ones INSTALLS - a round trip reports it - but is bitwise IDENTICAL to carrying no per-forest weight at all, the null gate its multiplicative composition (\(m_f \times 1 = m_f\)) is built to guarantee. The weight does not ride the sampler's saved state - a sampler rebuilt with setState from a stored state silently drops it while statesAgree still reports agreement - so it is additionally mirrored on an R5 field that getPointer, setState, and copy all reinstall on every re-creation; a caller never reinstalls it by hand. setData needs no clearing rule here the way it does for active: it is refused outright on any multi-forest sampler (“a multi-forest sampler fixes its data at creation”), so the two channels never interact.

active

A numeric vector of per-observation 0/1 membership indicators - "row \(i\) is not in the data set for this sampler this sweep" - of length equal to that with which the sampler was created, or NULL. setActiveRows reaches every family, the four that refuse a weighted likelihood included: gaussian, Student-t, probit, ordinal, logistic, nbinom, and aft samplers all accept it, including a multi-forest (forests) sampler, whose forests share one response of whichever family it was built under. It is absolute and independent of weights, composing with it in either call order (\(w_i \times a_i\) in effect). NULL clears the mask (every row active). Length and NA are validated as for weights; the only legal values are exactly 0 and 1, and a fractional element refuses the WHOLE call and installs nothing. An all-ones vector reports success but installs NOTHING, clearing any previously installed mask - the OPPOSITE of weights on gaussian and logistic, where an all-ones vector installs and is measurably distinct from carrying no weights at all. One channel states membership, the other precision, and the two deliberately carry opposite degenerate-value policies. The response scale, the count center and a forest's default sd are held across a mask as across weights, unless the call carries updateScale = TRUE, and a linear or gp leaf's covariate standardization unless it carries updateStandardization = TRUE. On a probit, ordinal or nbinom sampler, whose 0/1 weights state membership too, activeRows holds only what setActiveRows installed, and a row either channel brings back in draws nothing at the call, the next sweep drawing its latent first.

An inactive row (active[i] == 0) contributes nothing to any leaf sufficient statistic, branch log-likelihood, birth-scan weight total, leaf parameter draw, or family-level parameter update that sums over rows (residual degrees of freedom, a shape statistic, a group's per-group sums, and so on). It still occupies its leaf for COUNT-based accounting - numObservations, the birth scan's own member count, and leaf collapsing, which triggers on member count regardless of weights - and it still receives a fitted value: run()$train, getForestFits, getFitsWithoutOffset, and predict report \(f(x_i)\) at an inactive row exactly as at an active one, which is what makes this channel worth more than physically dropping the row. The rule that rejects a tree move leaving a leaf empty is count-based too: an inactive row is in the design but not in the likelihood, so a leaf all of whose rows are inactive is legal, takes no likelihood term and has its value drawn from the leaf prior, and the trees a sampler may hold do not depend on the mask. That is what lets a larger sampler that redraws the mask every sweep, from each row's conditional given the fit, sample the joint model it assumes. Its cost is that a fit under a fixed mask is close to the fit on the active rows alone but is not that fit, by the amounts given under weights. With every row inactive every leaf is such a leaf, which is the exact sense in which the forest “sits at its prior” - a distribution over structures, not a frozen one.

An inactive row's own latent draw is SKIPPED - no random numbers are consumed for it - for every family except Student-t, whose per-row \(\lambda_i\) is drawn unconditionally at every row regardless of the mask; there the mask instead ANNIHILATES its contribution through the composed weight (\(w_i \lambda_i a_i\)). For a skipping family, getLatents at an inactive row returns its LAST DRAWN value, which is stale; the correct read at an inactive row is its fit, not its latent. A stale latent does not come back into the likelihood: each sweep draws the latent of every row the mask holds in, for Student-t its \(\lambda_i\) of every row, from the row's conditional given the fit and before its trees, so a row switched back in is drawn afresh against the current fit with the rest. setActiveRows itself draws nothing and consumes no random numbers, whatever it switches, so a caller that draws the mask from the fit with the latents integrated out (a probit row's membership from its Bernoulli likelihood, say) need not call setResponse to refresh them. A multinomial sampler holds no latent between sweeps. A state installed over a different mask keeps, at rows that were out when it was stored, the latents they left with until the next sweep draws the rows the mask now holds in.

An inactive row's pointwise log-likelihood - the value the flat C API's logLikelihood results field reports (see ‘Mutation cost’ above for the C interface) - is NaN rather than a finite value or -Inf: a row that is not in the model has no likelihood to report.

Three quantities do NOT follow the mask, by design, so a caller wanting them recomputed on the active subset must re-create the sampler instead: the split-candidate cut grid stays the FULL-data grid, holding the tree prior fixed while the row set moves; the response transform and residual prior scale stay creation's calibration (a masked gaussian - and so aft, and any variance decoration - keeps the range and residual-prior scale creation set, which were taken over the rows in the likelihood then, every row when none was out); and an ordinal sampler keeps its FULL-data number of categories, free thresholds, and log-gap prior even when a mask empties a boundary category - only setData changes them. setData also CLEARS an installed mask - the mask is a per-row vector and setData may change the number of rows - so a caller replacing the data must reinstall any mask it wants kept.

The mask does not ride a sampler's saved state - the state carries derived quantities and no raw conditioning vector - so, exactly as setForestWeights's per-forest weight is, it is mirrored on an R5 field that getPointer, setState and copy all reinstall on every re-creation: a masked sampler saved and reloaded goes on masked, and a caller never reinstalls it by hand. What the mirror cannot do is travel with the state itself. Installing a stored state into a DIFFERENT sampler object leaves that object's own mask in force, whatever the donor's was - a destination that never had one stays unmasked and computes different draws while statesAgree still reports agreement - since the state holds no mask for the restore to re-derive against. Conversely, the latents DO ride the state, and under an installed mask they are stale at every inactive row for a skipping family, so two samplers at the same posterior state but different mask histories carry different stored latents and statesAgree correctly reports DISAGREEMENT; a Student-t sampler is affected the same way, since an inactive row's stored \(\lambda_i\) is drawn from a conditional its own data no longer informs.

basis

The data the named forest's amplitudes multiply, with as many rows as the sampler was created with and one amplitude per column. It is a value, or a one-sided formula, which is read as the basis of a forest is, its names found where the formula was written. It must be of the class the forest was created with, which decides what the forest multiplies and never changes. A forest of levels, created with a factor, a character vector or a logical vector, takes one of those three, matched to the forest's levels by name and not by position: the replacement may list its levels in another order or leave one out, a level of the forest that no row has is a column of zeros, and a row at a level the forest does not have, or at NA, is refused. Coefficient \(j\) multiplies level \(j\)'s rows after any swap, whatever the replacement declares. Numbers are refused for such a forest, the level indicators the sampler stores among them: to hand a basis back, hand back the factor. A forest of numbers takes one numeric column, a vector or a matrix of one column, a column of zeros among them, and refuses several columns, a factor, a character vector and a logical vector; as.numeric() of a logical vector is its 0/1 column. A forest created with no basis takes none. The sampler keeps the forest's block, one column for each level of a factor with no reference level dropped, in data@bases[[f]], and its levels in data@basis.levels[[f]], f the forest's position (neither list has names, so a label does not index them), and not the factor it was handed: a caller that will hand a basis back, to restore a proposal it rejected, keeps the factor it handed over. No forest changes width, held or drawn, so the names its columns were created with stay, whatever names the replacement has. The forest's label does not change. Unlike creation, a swap may leave a level of the forest with no row, and a numeric basis may hold a column of all zeros, the amplitude moving under its prior alone until a row takes it again, so a swap inside a larger sampler can leave a level or an arm momentarily unobserved; creation drops a level no row has and refuses a column of zeros. setForestBasis is the sole route by which a basis changes after creation, and it applies only to a sampler whose forests carry amplitudes, built with forests = (see dbarts). The amplitudes are preserved: an install leaves every one of them bitwise. A swap moves the basis and nothing else: no forest's prior moves, so a numeric forest keeps the sd per unit its creation gave it, a default one the scale of the column it was created on (data@basis.scale), unless updateBasisScale = TRUE takes the default of the new column. A basis that is not one of the canonical shapes (a dense all-ones column, or a complementary 0/1 pair) moves that forest onto the general amplitude conditional, which is a model fact and not revertible by a later data swap. The matrix is written to both the engine and data@bases, so getPointer's transparent re-creation after save/load carries the current assignment rather than the one the sampler was created with; because the bases ride creation, a swap applied after a state restore preserves the restored amplitudes. A state records the levels of each forest a factor multiplies, and setState puts each of its coefficients on this sampler's level of the same name, refusing a state whose names differ (see ‘Saving’). This draws nothing; the next sweep draws the augmentation variables against the change.

updateBasisScale

For setForestBasis, TRUE or FALSE, the default. TRUE, meant for burn-in, also takes the default of a numeric forest that states no sd from the column installed: the column's standard deviation is read over the observations in the likelihood at the call (a positive weight, kept by the active-row mask; a forest's own weights from setForestWeights are not read), and the forest's sd becomes one unit of the response's scale for one standard deviation of the new column, from the next sweep, as for a sampler created on that column over those observations (see sd in forest). The trees, the coefficients and every other forest are left as they are, and no draw is taken. The rows read are those in at the call, which may not be the rows the response's scale was read from at creation, and re-installing the column in force with TRUE is how to take its scale again after the weights or the mask change. The new scale replaces the forest's entry of data@basis.scale, so a copy, a saved and reloaded sampler and a sampler made again from its own control, model and data run the new prior. Where fewer than two observations are in the likelihood, the column takes one value over them, or the weights are counts that total at most 1 over them, the column is installed and the scale in force kept, with a warning the first time the sampler keeps a scale; a sampler created on such a column with no sd is refused. TRUE is refused, before anything is installed, on a forest that states its sd, at creation or through setLeafPrior, and on a forest multiplied by a factor, neither having a default taken from a column.

forest

A single positive integer indexing the forests from 1, or a string, the forest's label (see forest; forest<i> names position i, a sampler of one forest has no labels, and a multinomial one's are the response's levels), or - for getForestFits, getForestAmplitudes, getForestVariableCounts, getLeafPrior, and getK - NULL (the default on all five) for every forest, stacked (see ‘Value’ for each reader's stacked shape). A single-forest sampler's NULL read is bitwise its forest = 1 read, so the default costs nothing on an ordinary sampler. setForestWeights and setForestBasis have no default: a writer names one target rather than reading every one. setLeafPrior takes no forest: a multinomial sampler's normal(k = ) states every category forest, and a sampler whose forests carry amplitudes states one forest's size through setForest. setForest and getForest read their forest as the others do, left out on a sampler of one forest and on a multinomial one, whose setForest refuses a position or a level: its forests take one statement. Declared in that order, a Bayesian causal forest's prognostic forest is 1 and its basis forest 2; setForestWeights and setForestBasis are both refused on a sampler whose forests carry no amplitudes, but not with the same message - setForestWeights names the missing capability, while setForestBasis raises "forest index out of range" - and setForestBasis accepts any forest of one that does. getForestFits and getForestVariableCounts accept forest = 1 on any sampler - it selects the only forest - and refuse only an out-of-range index. getLeafPrior and getK are likewise served on every forest of a multi-forest sampler, and the calibration-map entries are that forest's own. getTrees takes the same forest = NULL default, stacking every forest forest-major with a leading forest column on a sampler with several forests or one declared with forests =, and no such column on any other (see ‘Value’); it additionally accepts a vector of forest indices or of labels, each validated as a lone forest argument is here and stacked in the order given. plotTree takes a single forest, defaulting to the sampler's only one and required when there is more than one.

leaf.prior

For setLeafPrior, a leaf prior specification in the vocabulary a fitting function's leaf.prior takes, resolved inside the call as it is there: normal(sd = ), normal(k = ), normal(sd = invchi(df, scale)), or linear(sd = ) and gp(sd = ) on those leaf models (see dbartsPriors). It must name the sampler's own leaf model - normal for the constant and monotone leaves - and may omit leaf-model details such as a linear leaf's columns; any it states must match. Changing the leaf model, or anything else about the model, is setModel's. A multinomial sampler takes normal(k = ) with a fixed k, Inf included, as its creation does. On any sampler normal(k = Inf) holds every tree at zero, so the fit is the offset, plus on a continuous response the center of the range the response less its offset spans. On a sampler whose forests carry amplitudes it is the fitting function's leaf prior; see ‘Value’.

sd, power, base, amplitude, proposal.probs, n.perturb.cuts, treeShift

For setForest, and of them power, base, proposal.probs and n.perturb.cuts for setVarianceForest, a value in the terms forest takes it, a coefficient's prior resolved inside the call as it is there. For setTreePrior, power and base in the terms a fitting function (dbarts) takes them. NULL, the default, is the same as leaving the name out. See ‘Value’.

split.probs

For setTreePrior, the split probabilities in the terms a fitting function takes them: a vector, 1 for equal probabilities, or on a DART sampler dart(...). NULL, the default, leaves them.

cuts

For setCutPoints, a numeric vector of cut points for the column named, or a list of such vectors, one for each column named; a data frame is taken as the list of its columns. A vector holds no NA or NaN and is sorted if it is out of order. A cut point must be finite; -.Machine$double.xmax separates values at -Inf. A point may appear only once, so a grid with a repeated point is refused; for more splits near a value, give a denser grid around it. No grid a sampler holds repeats a point, so the grids it reports can be handed back to it whole. A grid given here is unweighted, its cut points equally likely, except the grid the column holds handed back bit for bit, which keeps the weights the default rule gives a column with fewer distinct values than n.cuts. With column missing, cuts is a list with one entry for every column of the predictors, and the entries of factor columns are not read, whatever they are. Cut points apply to numeric predictors only: naming a factor column of either kind is refused, naming the kind, its grid following its level table rather than any externally chosen one. A later setState does not undo the change: a state goes onto the cut points the sampler holds (see ‘Saving’). The sampler records a grid set this way in its data object, so a later setData(sampler$data) keeps it; a later setData that derives the cut points, as one given a data object made by dbartsData does, derives every numeric column's cut points again whatever grid was set, at most as many as the n.cuts the sampler was created with: with useQuantiles, a column with no more distinct values than n.cuts gets one cut point fewer than it has distinct values, and a constant column gets one.

column

An integer or character string vector specifying which column/columns of the predictor matrix is to be replaced or for which cuts should be used. When updating predictors, it can be missing and the entire matrix will be substituted; a sparse or mixed dense/sparse design accepts that too, and keeps its storage (the replacement is spliced into the container rather than replacing it with a plain matrix). Such a design may equally be mutated one column at a time by naming column (dense-backed and sparse-backed columns alike, and a single call may name both kinds), which is the cheaper spelling when only a few columns move. A replaced sparse-backed column stays sparse: it stores the replacement's entries that differ from its implicit value (zero, or a sparse factor's reference level), in the storage layout chosen at creation, and a sparse column of the replacement is read as those entries rather than expanded, so for sparse columns the call's memory follows their nonzeros; a dense column of a mixed replacement is copied, as in any dense replacement. A replacement of any other sparse Matrix class is read as the dgCMatrix it holds, as is such a test set. For setTestPredictor, a per-column update reaches a data-frame or sparse test container too: the replacement is spliced into its storage rather than densifying the whole test set.

forceUpdate

For setPredictor, controls how the trees respond to a new predictor that would leave a leaf empty in any tree of any forest of any chain - the ordinary mean forest, and, on a sampler with more than one forest, all of them together: a Bayesian causal forest's second (treatment) forest, a multinomial sampler's per-category forests, and a heteroscedastic (variance) sampler's variance forest are checked on exactly the same terms as the mean forest, not independently (see ‘Multi-forest and heteroscedastic predictor mutation’ below). FALSE rolls the whole update back and leaves the sampler unchanged (rejection sampling); TRUE forces the change, collapsing any empty nodes; the string "partial" installs each observation's new value individually and rolls back only those observations whose value would empty a leaf in any of those trees, returning a per-observation logical of what was installed. Under a monotone constraint a new predictor can also leave a tree's leaf values out of order along a constrained predictor (that page says what this is). TRUE completes such an update, setting every leaf value of that tree to zero without a message; the next iteration draws them again. FALSE refuses it and rolls it back, as for an empty leaf, and "partial" declines each row that would do it. The one unforced change that can do this is an unordered factor column's first missing value, under the sides drawn for the column's rules when it arrives (see monotone). "partial" requires a single column and cannot be combined with updateCutPoints; it also requires a dense-backed column, since a sparse column's storage fixes its nonzero pattern per cell - replace such a column whole instead. When missing, defaults to TRUE when the whole predictor matrix is being replaced (column is missing) and FALSE when a single column is being replaced.

For setState, a single TRUE or FALSE. FALSE, the default, installs a state only where no tree of it has to be changed to fit the sampler, and otherwise leaves the sampler as it was; TRUE installs it, repairing the trees that do not fit (see ‘Saving’). "partial" is not taken.

For installTrees, FALSE (the default) takes the donor only if every tree it gives can stand in this sampler as the donor holds it, and TRUE takes it changing what must be changed (see ‘Warm starts’).

updateCutPoints

For setPredictor, one of "none", "position" or "value", or a unique abbreviation of one. "none", the default, keeps the cut points (split candidate locations) of the replaced column(s) and the weights they carry. The other two derive them again from the new values, as a new sampler would for those values: up to the n.cuts the sampler holds, whatever number the column held, and fewer where the values supply fewer, a constant column getting one, and under the default rule one per gap, weighted by width, on a column with fewer distinct values than n.cuts. They differ in where the splits already on such a column go. Under "position" each keeps its position on the grid, which is what TRUE did in 0.9-x; when the number of cut points changes, the position is rescaled to the new number. Under "value" each moves to the new cut point nearest its old threshold. In either case a split stays between the splits above it in its tree; one left with no cut point there is merged when the update is forced, and otherwise the update is refused and rolled back, trees and cut points included. A later setState does not bring back the cut points a state was stored on (see ‘Saving’). Anything but "none" cannot be combined with forceUpdate = "partial". For setData the same three words, or NULL, the default: "none" keeps the sampler's cut points and their weights, the new values read on them, "position" and "value" derive them from the new data as above, and NULL takes the cutPoints the new data object records, a split on a column whose cut points that changes moving to the nearest of them, and otherwise derives them as "value" does, as setData always did. For setPredictor, a logical is taken until dbarts 1.1-0, TRUE as "position" and FALSE as "none", with a warning once per session (dbarts-deprecated).

updateStandardization

For setPredictor, FALSE, the default, keeps a linear or gp leaf's covariate standardization, each covariate's center and scale and a gp leaf's heuristic lengthscale, whatever values the update installs; TRUE derives it again for the covariates among the columns the update replaces, every column where column is missing, over their new values at the rows in the likelihood under the weights and mask in force, as creation would over them, once the update has gone in, keeps the other covariates', and rewrites a linear leaf's coefficients, current and saved, into it, so that each leaf is the function of the covariate it was and predict returns what it did. A replaced covariate those rows hold at one value, or observe at none, keeps its numbers, and the call warns, with class dbartsScaleFallbackWarning, on the sampler's first keep, of this or of the response's scale (updateScale); on a hazard fit where fewer than two subjects are in, every replaced covariate keeps, the period among them, the warning counting subjects. For setData, NULL, the default, takes the standardization the new data object records and otherwise derives it from the new data's rows in, TRUE derives it, both reading every row where fewer than two rows are in or the response's scale is read from every row, and refused where two or more rows in hold one value of a covariate unless a gp leaf states its lengthscale, which takes the placeholder (see newData), and FALSE keeps the sampler's, the new rows read under it. A leaf that takes no covariate has nothing to derive. A gp sampler that holds saved draws refuses TRUE on setPredictor, and on setData any call that would change the standardization (see newData). It cannot be combined with forceUpdate = "partial".

For setWeights and setActiveRows, the argument after updateScale: FALSE, the default, keeps the standardization whatever rows the call leaves in; TRUE installs the weights or the mask first and then derives every leaf covariate's center and scale, and a gp leaf's heuristic lengthscale, again over the rows then in the likelihood, as setPredictor with TRUE would on every leaf covariate's values in force, rewriting a linear leaf's coefficients in the same way. A covariate those rows hold at one value, or observe at none, keeps its numbers, the others re-deriving, and the call warns as setPredictor does, once per sampler. On a hazard fit, where fewer than two subjects are in after the call, every covariate keeps its numbers, the period among them, which varies within a subject, under one warning that counts subjects. Where the call also passes updateScale = TRUE and keeps the response's scale, those rows holding fewer than two distinct values of the response, the prior in force is kept whole: every covariate keeps its numbers too, whatever its spread over those rows, and one warning names the response and the covariates, as creation on those rows would read the response's scale and the covariates from every row together. A gp sampler holding saved draws refuses it before anything is installed. A sampler whose leaves take no covariate, one of several forests among them, takes it and has nothing to derive. A probit, ordinal or nbinom sampler's setWeights passes it to setActiveRows with the 0/1 weights.

A loop whose rows in the likelihood change, such as a mixture component or an imputation step, can let the response's scale and the leaf covariates' center and scale follow the rows in during burn-in and then hold them, so every kept draw comes from one prior: pass updateScale and updateStandardization as TRUE on the call that changes the rows while burning in, and FALSE after. A gp leaf that has kept a draw refuses both, so burn in with sweeps that keep nothing:

sampler <- dbarts(y ~ x1 + x2, data, weights = w,
                  leaf.prior = linear("x1"),
                  control = dbartsControl(n.chains = 1L, keepTrees = TRUE))
for (i in seq_len(n.burn + n.keep)) {
  w <- drawMembership(sampler)            # the outer sampler's step
  burning <- i <= n.burn
  sampler$setWeights(w, updateScale = burning,
                     updateStandardization = burning)
  draw <- if (burning) sampler$run(1L, 0L) else sampler$run(0L, 1L)
}

Creation and a setData that derives read every row where fewer than two rows are in, or where the response's scale is read from every row, and refuse two or more rows in that hold one value of a leaf covariate, a gp leaf that states its lengthscale taking the placeholder (see newData); these setters keep instead, one row or one subject in included.

splits

For setCutPoints, "position" (the default) or "value", or a unique abbreviation: where the splits already on a column go when its cut points are replaced, as for updateCutPoints. The change is always forced, so a split left with no cut point between the splits above it is merged.

treeNums

An integer vector listing the indices of the trees to print or return.

chainNums

An integer vector listing the chains to return from getTrees. When missing, all chains are returned.

sampleNums

An integer vector listing the saved samples to return from getTrees or print from printTrees. Applies only when keepTrees is TRUE and current is FALSE; otherwise the live working trees have no sample dimension, and supplying it explicitly is ignored, with a warning. Sample numbers address recorded DRAWS on the oldest-first axis predict reports - 1 to the number of draws recorded, at most control@n.samples - and not the store's internal slots.

current

For getTrees, a logical; when TRUE the live working trees (the current sampler position) are returned even if keepTrees is TRUE, rather than the saved samples.

newdata

For getTrees, an optional matrix of predictors (in the form accepted by predict). When supplied, its observations are routed through each tree so the n column counts them instead of the training data; the tree structure, splits, and leaf values are unchanged.

result

For getLatents, an optional pre-allocated numeric vector (or, with multiple chains, matrix) that it fills in place and returns instead of allocating a new one; its length must equal the number of observations times the number of chains. Omit it to let getLatents allocate. Refused by name by getSigmas and getSumsOfSquaredResiduals: both readers allocate their own vector, and filling a caller's buffer in place is getLatents's contract alone.

test

For getVariance, a logical; FALSE, the default, reads the variance surface at the training rows and TRUE at the installed test rows.

treeNum

An integer listing the indices of the tree to plot.

chainNum

For plotTree, an integer giving the chain to plot from. Required when the sampler has more than one chain; defaults to 1 when there is only one.

sampleNum

For plotTree, an integer giving the saved sample to plot. Applies only when keepTrees is TRUE, in which case it defaults to the most recently drawn sample; ignored (with the live working trees plotted instead) when keepTrees is FALSE.

treePlotPars

A named numeric vector containing the quantities nodeHeight, nodeWidth, and nodeGap, all of which control aspects of the resulting plot.

donor

For installTrees, the fit whose forests seed this sampler: another dbartsSampler, or a bart object fit with keepSampler = TRUE. The donor must share this sampler's predictors; a donor of more trees gives some of them, and a donor on other cut points has its splits moved onto this sampler's under forceUpdate = TRUE, and needs no move where every split it holds is one of this sampler's cut points, as on a finer grid that holds the donor's; and a different center and scale of a linear leaf's covariates is allowed (see ‘Warm starts’).

samples

For installTrees, an optional integer vector with one entry per chain, each a 1-based index into the donor's pool of samples (its saved trees when it kept them, else its final trees per chain). NULL spreads the chains evenly across the pool.

n.sweeps

For growFromRoot, a single positive integer giving the number of grow-from-root sweeps run in place (default 2L). Each sweep rebuilds every tree in the forest against the current residual, so a small handful reaches a good fit.

ptr

For storeState, the sampler's engine pointer to capture from; defaults to getPointer() and is rarely passed explicitly.

newState

For setState, a state object previously produced by this sampler or another over the same data: its state field, calling storeState() first to refresh it if a later mutation may have gone unstored (storeState itself returns NULL invisibly, so its return value cannot be passed here). A sampler's own state field is never refused for the cut points it records: where a reload is made on other cut points than its stored state records, as after a setCutPoints with no storeState() since (see ‘Saving’), the field holds the state of its engine in place of the stored one. A reload's field is brought to its engine's at first use, and a state read from it before that is the stored one. Must inherit from bartcoreState. setState installs the latents the state carries, the values its trees were drawn from, and draws none.

n.trees, vars, interactions, blocks

For setForest (and n.trees and vars for setVarianceForest), the names forest takes that say what the model is. They are refused by name whatever their value, being part of the model, and are arguments so that a short name matches as it does at creation.

...

For setForest and setVarianceForest, nothing is taken: any name not listed is refused as an unused argument. For plotTree, extra arguments to plot. For run, only 0.9-x's per-call thread count, as n.threads, numThreads or the one unnamed argument after updateState, which is ignored with a once-per-session warning until dbarts 1.1-0 (dbarts-deprecated); anything else is refused. A callback to run must therefore be named.

Fields

Read with $, as the methods are called. Treat them as read-only: assigning to a field changes only the R-side copy and leaves the underlying engine untouched, so the sampler's behavior does not follow. Route changes through the set* methods instead.

control

The sampler's dbartsControl, carrying n.chains, n.threads, n.trees, keepTrees, updateState, and the rest. Replace with setControl.

model

A dbartsModel holding the parsed tree, leaf, and residual priors, together with any monotonicity, interaction, and block constraints. Replace with setModel.

data

A dbartsData holding the current predictors, response, test data, weights, and offset. Its x slot is stored columnar for data-frame input and so need not be a plain matrix; use extract(sampler, "predictors") for the numeric predictor matrix, which is what tree replay and getTrees count against. Replace with setData, or a piece at a time with the other set* methods.

state

The cached, serializable engine state, or NULL until one is materialized. It holds the chains and not the model: trees, leaf values, the quantities the sampler draws, the cut points the trees' split thresholds were stored on (the attribute cutPoints, a list with one entry per predictor column, NULL for a factor column that splits by subsets of its levels; with their weights, the attribute cutMass, where a column's cut points are not equally likely) and the leaf-covariate standardization they are read through, a record of the response mapping they were read under, which predictor columns could hold a missing value when it was stored, and the levels of each forest a factor multiplies (the attribute basisLevels) - no leaf prior and no value the sampler holds fixed (see ‘Saving’). It also carries each chain's generator state, so restoring it continues the same streams the sampler was drawing from, typically to the last few digits, not bitwise. The saved-tree store's write position and the number of draws it has recorded both ride it, so predict after a setState reports the same draws, in the same order, as before the store. Reading it forces the sampler's current state only the first time, before any value has been materialized; once set, it is a cached snapshot that a later mutation does not refresh automatically - call storeState again, or pass updateState = TRUE to the mutating call (see updateState above), to bring it forward. After a setState that put a state onto cut points, or weights of them, other than the ones the state records, the field holds the sampler's state as storeState() gives it and not the state as it was given, so that a copy or a reload has the sampler's cut points and trees. It is the only field save needs, and restoring one requires setState - see ‘Saving’.

pointer

The external pointer to the C++ engine. Internal; never manipulate it directly.

Details

A dbartsSampler is a mutable object which contains information pertaining to fitting a Bayesian additive regression tree model. The sampler is first created and then, in a separate instruction, run or modified. In this way, MCMC samplers can be constructed with BART components filling arbitrary roles.

Besides dbarts, a sampler is created by new("dbartsSampler", control, model, data, active = NULL) from the list dbartsSpec returns. The list's data object carries the fit's weights, a "probit", "ordinal" or "nbinom" fit's 0/1 weights among them, so a sampler created from it is the sampler dbarts builds (dbartsSpec, data, gives the by-hand route). active is a 0/1 mask installed once the sampler is built, as setActiveRows(active) installs it, composing with the weights; a sampler created with it reads over the rows in, those the weights and the mask both keep, the center of an "nbinom" count, a linear or gp leaf's covariate center and scale, and under "probit" and "logistic" the default sd of a forest on a numeric column that states none.

A sampler made this way takes its tree count from the model and its quantile rule and cut count from the data object, where they state them. A control that is fresh, or copied from a fit, says nothing of them, and a copied count or rule that differs draws a warning saying it is not used. A count or rule written on the control is used where the model or the data object states none and is refused, by name, where it states another, or, for a count, where every forest has a basis. Whether the family is binary is the model's family alone.

Reading the fit

Six methods report a fitted quantity and no two report the same one. They differ along three axes - the SCALE the values live on, whether the installed OFFSET is in them, and whether they answer from the CURRENT state or from stored draws:

methodscaleoffsetcurrent or stored
run()$trainresponse (latent under a binary family)includedone slab per recorded draw
$getFitsWithoutOffset()response (latent under a binary family)excludedcurrent
$getForestFits(f)internal, and one forest onlyexcludedcurrent
$predict(x)response (latent under a binary family)whatever you pass itthe saved samples under keepTrees, else the current trees
$predictForests(x)internal, one channel per forestexcluded, and refused if passedthe saved samples under keepTrees, else the current trees
$getLatents()the family's own augmentation variable, which is a location for some families and a precision for othersnot a fit; see ‘Value’current

A multinomial (softmax) sampler reads and writes a strict subset of this surface, by the model rather than by omission. Its response channels are $setResponse, which takes the \(n \times K\) count matrix, $setCategoryOffset and $setCategoryTestOffset; the predictor family ($setPredictor in all four shapes, $setCutPoints, $setTestPredictor) and the global $setActiveRows are open, and $predict answers with the \(K\) category probabilities and takes the matching per-category offset. Everything else on the mutation surface is refused, each by a message naming the capability and, where one exists, the channel that serves the caller instead: $setResponse given a vector and $setOffset (a flat vector cannot express the matrix, and a flat shift is the softmax's null direction), $setActiveRows at updateScale = TRUE (the categories keep their scale at creation), $setWeights (an integer case weight is already row-wise replication in the count response, and a non-integer one has no exact augmentation sampler), $setSigma (no residual scale), $setData and $setModel (the K category forests fix their data and their calibration at creation), a named sd or a k hyperprior on $setLeafPrior, which takes normal(k = ) with a fixed k (the softmax map owns every category forest's leaf scale), $setForestWeights and $setForestBasis (its forests are its categories, which carry no amplitudes), and $getFitsWithoutOffset (its reported channels are probabilities, not one additive location). Per-forest masking is refused permanently rather than pending: a category's margin is a log-sum-exp over the other \(K-1\), so a mask on one forest alone has no conditional to be a mask of.

The composition rule follows from the table: an outer block conditions on \(f(x_i)\), so it reads $getFitsWithoutOffset() and adds back whatever offset it installed, rather than differencing $getLatents() against run()$train: a probit, ordinal or aft latent is on the offset-inclusive scale, \(z = f(x) + o + e\), as run()$train is, so the difference is the residual \(e\) with none of the offset's signal. A block that owns the offset regresses z - $getFitsWithoutOffset(); a precision latent carries no location and no offset, and dbartsWorkingResponse gives the offset-free working response.

Where the boundary runs.
